claims.text: The starting material is equimolar CoCrFeNiTi in a single-phase solid-solution state with large grains or a single-crystal structure and minimal defects.
Single-phase CoCrFeNiTi has relatively low hardness and strength while retaining favorable plasticity and machinability.
Adding Ti to CoCrFeNi raises the stacking-fault energy.
The elevated stacking-fault energy promotes facile cross-slip and dislocation mobility.
Ti lowers lattice friction in equimolar CoCrFeNiTi.
Ti facilitates activation of multiple slip systems in equimolar CoCrFeNiTi.
A homogeneous single-phase matrix supports rapid dynamic recovery through dislocation annihilation and rearrangement.
Rapid dynamic recovery prevents significant dislocation storage and accumulation.
Reduced dislocation accumulation suppresses pile-up and forest hardening.
Suppressed forest hardening explains the alloy's low hardness and strength despite favorable plasticity.
A comparison with Ti-free CoCrFeNi having matched microstructure and test conditions isolates the effect of Ti.
In situ TEM straining can expose deformation mechanisms and dynamic defect behavior during loading.
Digital image correlation can directly quantify dislocation arrangement, annihilation, and subgrain formation.
Relative to Ti-free CoCrFeNi, CoCrFeNiTi will have lower yield stress and flow stress.
CoCrFeNiTi will show faster dislocation motion and less dislocation accumulation than Ti-free CoCrFeNi.
Interrupted tests will show accelerated dynamic recovery in CoCrFeNiTi, including lower strain-hardening rates at lower strain rates.
The proposed mechanism applies at room temperature under uniaxial loading from 10^-4 to 10^-2 s^-1 when grain size, orientation, and secondary-phase differences are minimized.
The relative contributions of cross-slip facilitation and dynamic-recovery rate are not yet quantified.
Failure to observe faster mobility or enhanced recovery in CoCrFeNiTi relative to the Ti-free control would falsify the proposed mechanism.
